title: The four truths, now
hook: dukkha, its cause, its end, the path, as you understand them now
tomorrow: why did the Buddha give brahmins a road to Brahma?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three jewels: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha, three places to rest. Today, the dhamma itself, the way the Buddha packed it into four lines.
screen: `THREE PLACES TO REST.` → `THE DHAMMA, IN FOUR LINES.`

segments.voice: A grove of simsapa trees near Kosambi, leaves underfoot and leaves overhead. The Buddha was staying there with his monks. He bent down, picked up a few fallen leaves, held them out to the monks, and asked: which are more, these leaves in my hand, or the leaves in the trees above us? The ones above, they said. Many more. So it is, he told them, with what I've known and not taught you. So which few leaves did he keep in his hand?
screen: `A GROVE NEAR KOSAMBI.` → `A FEW LEAVES IN HIS HAND.` → `WHICH ARE MORE?` → `WHAT DID HE KEEP?`

segments.voice: His answer, in the Samyutta Nikaya, is plain. He left the rest untaught because it didn't help: it didn't lead to letting go, to peace, to awakening. What he did teach was four things. This is dukkha: the ache in things, the way even good things won't hold still. This is its arising: craving, the thirst that keeps wanting more, or wanting other. This is its ending: when the thirst lets go, the ache ends with it, and Buddhists call that nirvana. And this is the path to its ending: the noble eightfold path. These are the four noble truths, and the suttas put them at the heart of his first sermon, to five companions in the deer park near Benares. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says them in one breath: "pain, the origin of pain, the destruction of pain, and the eightfold holy way that leads to the quieting of pain." Some teachers read the four like a doctor's visit: what's wrong, what's causing it, can it end, and the treatment. Read that way, the first three point at the fourth. That's why the line today says one path. The handful hasn't grown in five years. What this path has added is the walking: the breath, the precepts, the sits, the kindness, each one a piece of the fourth.
screen: `ONLY WHAT HELPS.` · `THE ACHE, THE THIRST.` · `THE ENDING, AND THE WAY.` · `THREE POINT TO THE FOURTH.` · then, large: `FOUR TRUTHS, ONE PATH.`

segments.voice: Pick up four small things near you, leaves if you have them, or coins, or pens. Lay them in your open palm one at a time, and as each one lands, name a truth in your own words, as if to someone across a kitchen table: the ache, its cause, its ending, the way. Then close your hand gently and sit with the fourth.
The four truths: dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the path. The handful of leaves the Buddha chose to keep in his hand.
Keep this one: four truths, one path, and the path is the part you walk. Nine days up the summit.

fork.setup: a friend says, 'Buddhism is just pessimism: life is suffering, the end.' which part of the four truths answers that best?
options: the third and fourth: the ache can end, and there's a path to it.
the first: if you look closely, the ache isn't really there at all.
the second: craving is good, because it keeps people going.
fork.reveal: the Buddha didn't stop at dukkha. the third truth is its ending, and the fourth is the way there.

chat.meaning: In the simsapa grove the Buddha kept a handful of leaves: dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the path. The first three point to the fourth.

tie.story: The Buddha held up a few simsapa leaves and said what he taught was only that handful: the four truths.
tie.friend: Mai can give her roommate the handful in one text: the ache, its cause, its ending, the path.
tie.you: how would you say the four truths in your own words?

simsapa.meaning: a kind of tree; the grove where he held up the leaves

Kosambi.meaning: an old city in India where the grove stood

dukkha.meaning: the ache in things: stress, unease, suffering

nirvana.meaning: the ending of craving and the ache; Pali nibbana

Benares.meaning: the city now called Varanasi, near the deer park

notes: SN 56.31 paraphrased: at Kosambi in the simsapa grove the Buddha takes up a few leaves; what he has directly known but not taught is like the leaves overhead; he taught what is beneficial and leads to disenchantment, peace and awakening, namely the four noble truths. Confirm wording of the paraphrase.
SN 56.11: the first sermon to the group of five monks at the deer park at Isipatana near Baranasi (Benares). Confirm 'deer park near Benares' is acceptable.
Dhammapada 190-191 quoted from Max Müller 1881; confirm exact wording.
The doctor's-visit reading is labeled 'some teachers read'; it is a later teaching analogy, not a sutta claim. Confirm framing.
